1219.title: The robe not passed on
1219.hook: Huineng said the robe would no longer be handed down; the teaching itself is the proof
1219.howItsDone: Zen and Chan schools speak of the teaching passing from teacher to student, often called mind-to-mind transmission, and the story of Huiming at the mountain pass is often retold, with 'original face' used as a koan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sudden awakening, and the sutra's reminder that the teaching itself has no speeds. Your line: sudden and gradual.

Some families have one object that matters more than anything else in the house. A watch. A ring. A recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting. It's meant to be handed down, a sign that the line goes on. And some families know the other side of that story: the cousins who stopped speaking over who got the watch. The thing meant to hold the family together became the thing it split over. Chan had an object like that too: a robe, handed from teacher to student. And in the Platform Sutra, someone decides it should stop.
screen: `ONE OBJECT THAT MATTERS.` → `A SIGN THE LINE GOES ON.` → `THE THING THEY SPLIT OVER.`

segments.voice: After the two verses on the wall, the sutra says, Hongren calls Huineng in secret, teaches him, and hands him the robe and bowl as the sign of the teaching. He tells him to leave that same night and go south, because people may try to harm him. And he says, in paraphrase: the robe has become a cause of strife. Let it stop with you. Monks set off after Huineng to take the robe back. One of them, a former military officer named Huiming, catches up at a mountain pass. Huineng lays the robe on a rock and steps aside. In the sutra, Huiming tries to pick it up and cannot lift it. Then he says: I came for the teaching, not for the robe. And Huineng gives him one, in paraphrase: not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, right at this moment, what is your original face? Huiming, the sutra says, awakens on the spot. The man who ran up a mountain for a piece of cloth goes home with something nobody can carry off. Late in the sutra, near the end of his life, Huineng tells his students the robe will not be handed down. The proof that the teaching is alive won't be an object anyone can fight over. It will be the teaching itself, showing up in the people who practice it. The robe stops here, so that the teaching doesn't have to.
screen: `ROBE AND BOWL, AT NIGHT.` · `A CHASE TO THE MOUNTAIN PASS.` · `I CAME FOR THE TEACHING.` · `THE TEACHING IS THE PROOF.` · then, large: `THE ROBE STOPS HERE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you know how to do that could never be handed over in a box: how to apologize properly, how to wait for the bread to rise, how to sit with someone who's grieving. Notice where it lives, in the hands, in the timing, in the voice. Nobody could lay it on a rock, and nobody could carry it off.
The robe not passed on. In the Platform Sutra, the robe that had become a cause of strife stops with Huineng, and the teaching itself carries on. Today's word.

1220.title: Meditation and wisdom are one
1220.hook: Huineng: like a lamp and its light, meditation and wisdom are one
1220.howItsDone: Zen and Chan teachers often cite Huineng's lamp and light when they explain that sitting is not only a way to calm down before insight, but already a form of clear seeing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the robe not passed on: the thing people fought over stopped with Huineng, and the teaching went on. Your line: the robe stops here.

Which comes first, the lamp or its light? It sounds like a riddle for children, and then it doesn't. Strike a match and touch it to a wick. Is there a moment when the flame is burning but not yet giving light? When the light is shining with no flame behind it? Try to find the seam. There isn't one. Huineng reached for exactly this picture to show how two parts of practice fit together, the quiet part and the seeing part.
screen: `THE LAMP OR ITS LIGHT?` → `A FLAME TOUCHES A WICK.` → `TRY TO FIND THE SEAM.`

segments.voice: In the Platform Sutra, Huineng tells his listeners that his teaching rests on two things, often translated meditation and wisdom. Meditation here means the steadiness of a settled mind. Wisdom means clear seeing. It's natural to treat them as a sequence: first I'll get calm, and once I'm calm enough, insight will come. Huineng says, in paraphrase, don't be confused into thinking they are different. People who say meditation first and then wisdom, or wisdom first and then meditation, have already split them in two. Then the lamp. In paraphrase again: meditation and wisdom are like a lamp and its light. Where there is a lamp, there is light. Where there is no lamp, there is darkness. The lamp is the body of the light, and the light is what the lamp does. They have two names, he says, but one substance. If they're one, then steadiness is not a waiting room you sit in until wisdom shows up. A steady moment is already a seeing moment. When you pause before answering an angry text, the pause isn't just calm. It's also where you see what the text actually says. Huineng's word for the relationship is body and function, and it fits with his no-thought: the mind doesn't go blank to become wise. Its stillness is already giving light.

segments.voice: If you have a candle or a small lamp nearby, and it's safe to, light it and set it in front of you; if not, any light will do, a window or a screen dimmed low. Rest your eyes on it, watch steadily, and see whether, while you're watching steadily, you're also seeing clearly. Look for the seam between the steadiness and the seeing.

1221.title: Searching for the ox
1221.hook: the ten oxherding pictures: first, a herdsman searches for a lost ox
1221.howItsDone: Some Zen and Chan teachers use the oxherding pictures in talks and retreats as a map of practice, and students often study the pictures, prefaces and poems one stage at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Huineng's teaching that meditation and wisdom are one. Your line: the lamp and its light.

A man stands at the edge of a field of wild grass, a rope in his hand. The grass is high. Beyond it, a river, and past the river, mountains. Somewhere out there is his ox, and it's gone. He pushes through the grass, crosses the water, climbs, and keeps going until the paths blur together and his legs give out. Evening comes. Nothing. No ox, no hoofprint, just cicadas in the trees as the light goes. That's the whole of the first picture in a series Chan and Zen have used to draw the way itself.
screen: `A MAN WITH A ROPE.` → `GRASS, RIVER, MOUNTAINS.` → `ONLY CICADAS AT DUSK.`

segments.voice: The oxherding pictures this path follows are a set of ten images, each with a short prose preface and a short poem. Tradition credits this set to a Chan teacher named Kuoan, known in Japan as Kakuan. They follow a herdsman and his ox from loss, through finding and taming, all the way home and beyond, and over the coming days this path walks them one at a time. The first poem, in paraphrase: busily parting the endless grasses, he searches. The rivers are wide, the mountains far, the path keeps going. Worn out, he finds nothing, and hears only the cicadas in the evening maples. Effort, with no result yet. Then the twist, in the preface. In paraphrase: the ox has never gone missing. So why search? Because the herdsman turned his back on awakening, the ox became a stranger to him and got lost in the dust. Far from home, he stands at a crossroads, and gain and loss flare up in him like fire, right and wrong like a thicket of spears. Some readers hear the ox as the herdsman's own true nature: never really gone, only turned away from. Why start here? It would be easy to skip this picture and want the finding. But the first step is admitting the search is on, and naming it. Everything that follows begins with someone out in the grass, looking.
screen: `A SERIES OF TEN PICTURES.` · `THE FIRST: ALONE IN TALL GRASS.` · `THE OX WAS NEVER LOST.` · `THE SEARCH, NAMED.` · then, large: `SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself gently: what am I searching for? Not the polished answer, the real one, peace or approval or rest or something without a name yet; when it comes, name it simply, in a word or two, and don't argue with it. Then let the question go and rest with the breath, the way the herdsman might finally sit down at dusk and listen to the cicadas.
Searching for the ox. The first of the oxherding pictures: a herdsman alone in the grasses, looking for an ox the preface says was never lost. Today's word.
Your line: searching. Every picture after this one starts out here in the grass. Go gently.

1222.title: Seeing the tracks
1222.hook: second picture: he finds the ox's footprints in the teachings
1222.howItsDone: Zen teachers often use the oxherding pictures in talks and retreats as a map of practice, and students reflect on which picture describes where they are; the second picture is commonly read as learning about the way through study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first oxherding picture: a herdsman out in the tall grass, searching for an ox the preface says was never lost. Your line: searching.

A muddy riverbank keeps a footprint for a while. Farmers learn to read those marks, and so does anyone who has lost a dog in the woods: how deep the print sinks, which way the toes point, how fresh the edges look. A print is not the animal. But it tells you the animal is real, that it came this way, and that you're not chasing a rumor. In the second oxherding picture, the herdsman looks down and sees prints in the mud.
screen: `A FOOTPRINT IN THE MUD.` → `NOT THE ANIMAL, BUT PROOF IT'S REAL.` → `THE SECOND PICTURE.`

segments.voice: First, where the tracks are. The short preface says the herdsman finds them through the sutras and the teachings. He reads, he asks, he listens to people who have walked this way, and something starts to make sense. That's the footprint: not the ox, but real evidence that there is an ox. Second, a track is not the ox. He has found traces, the preface says, but he has not yet entered the gate. He can talk about the ox, even explain its prints well to someone else. An old Buddhist image says it another way: a finger pointing at the moon. The teaching points; the trap is staring at the finger. Third, it still counts as a step. In the first picture there were no prints at all. Now there's a direction. The verse says, in paraphrase, that the prints are scattered along the stream and under the trees, and however far the ox wanders into the hills, its nose reaches the sky; it can't be hidden. Fourth, tracks on an ordinary day. A line from a talk stays with you for a week. A friend meets bad news with a steadiness that's hard to explain. A few quiet minutes in the morning change the afternoon. None of these is awakening. Each is a print in the mud, a sign the way is real and runs somewhere. The herdsman hasn't arrived, and he isn't making it up.

segments.voice: Look back over the last few weeks for one track: a moment, a line, a person, a small habit that seemed to point somewhere. A small print is still a print, so don't weigh whether it's big enough. Rest your attention on it, the way the herdsman crouches by the mud, and notice which way it points.

1223.title: Seeing the ox
1223.hook: third picture: he glimpses the ox itself
1223.howItsDone: In Zen communities the third oxherding picture is often read as a first direct glimpse of one's own nature, and teachers use it to remind students that such a glimpse is real but is the start of training, not the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the second picture: prints in the mud, signs of the ox found in the teachings, but not yet the ox itself. Your line: the tracks.

A bird sings somewhere in the branches. The sun is warm, the wind is soft, the willows along the bank are green. That's the verse for the third oxherding picture, and it's oddly ordinary. No thunder, no vision in the clouds. The herdsman has followed prints for a long time, reading about the ox, talking about the ox. Then, on a pleasant afternoon, he hears that bird, looks up, and there among the willows is the ox itself.
screen: `A BIRD SINGS. THE WILLOWS ARE GREEN.` → `AN ORDINARY AFTERNOON.` → `THE OX ITSELF.`

segments.voice: First, from evidence to contact. The preface says, in paraphrase, that he finds the way in through sound: hearing clearly opens the gate. Reading about honey and tasting it are different kinds of knowing, and this is the move from one to the other. Second, the glimpse comes through the senses, not around them. The verse keeps him right where he is: birdsong, sunlight, wind, willows. Some Zen teachers say the way isn't hidden behind daily life; it's shining through it. The verse even asks where the ox could possibly hide. Third, seen, but not yet caught. In some well-known drawings only part of the ox shows, its head or its hindquarters, the rest behind a tree. A glimpse can be completely real and still be brief. Fourth, now he knows for himself. Without a glimpse, all the tracks in the world stay secondhand. In ordinary life it can be very small: a moment where the mind is clear and nothing is missing, the sound of rain heard all the way through. It may pass in seconds. The third picture says that's enough to change the search, because the old question, is there even an ox, has been answered.
screen: `FROM EVIDENCE TO CONTACT.` · `THE GLIMPSE COMES THROUGH THE SENSES.` · `SEEN, BUT NOT YET CAUGHT.` · `NOW HE KNOWS FOR HIMSELF.` · then, large: `THERE IT IS.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest, and instead of looking for anything, let sound come to you, the way the bird's song came to the herdsman: the hum of a fridge, a car outside, your own breath. Hear one sound all the way through, from its start to its fading. If a moment comes that is simply clear, notice it without grabbing; if none comes, listening is still the practice.

1224.title: Catching the ox
1224.hook: fourth picture: he catches it, and it fights the rope
1224.howItsDone: Zen teachers often point to the fourth oxherding picture when students find that old habits return after a clear moment in practice, treating the struggle as a normal stage that calls for steady effort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third picture: birdsong, green willows, and a glimpse of the ox itself, seen but not caught. Your line: there it is.

What comes after a breakthrough? Stories about change usually stop at the moment of insight: the light comes on, the music swells, the credits roll. The oxherding pictures keep going. In the fourth picture the herdsman finally gets a rope around the ox. And the ox is not grateful to be found. It throws its head, it bolts, it drags him toward the hills. The rope goes taut in his hands.
screen: `A ROPE AROUND THE OX.` → `IT THROWS ITS HEAD AND BOLTS.` → `THE ROPE GOES TAUT.`

segments.voice: First, at last, the ox on a rope. After searching, tracks and a glimpse, the thing he's been looking for is no longer out in the grass. It's in his hands. Second, it's still wild. The preface, in paraphrase, says the ox has lived so long in the wilderness that it's hard to hold. It still longs for the sweet grass; its stubborn streak is still strong. Being caught doesn't erase the habits of all those years. A clear moment doesn't come with new reflexes. The old pulls are there the next morning: the scroll, the snap at someone you love, the worry that circles at night. Third, it pulls hard. The verse has him holding on with all his strength while the ox charges toward the high ground or drifts off into misty valleys. The picture doesn't scold the ox. A wild ox pulls. The struggle isn't a sign the glimpse was fake; it's what holding on looks like at first. Fourth, so he holds on. The preface says that to make the ox gentle, he'll need the whip. Some readers hear that as firmness, not cruelty: steady effort and attention, returning again and again. The fourth picture is the stage of grip. Tomorrow's is the stage of patience.
screen: `AT LAST, THE OX ON A ROPE.` · `LONG IN THE WILD, STILL WILD.` · `IT PULLS HARD. THAT'S WHAT OXEN DO.` · `SO HE HOLDS ON.` · then, large: `IT PULLS.`

segments.voice: Rest with the breath, and before long something will pull: an itch, a plan, a replayed argument, the urge to check the time. Don't fight it and don't follow it; stay with it, the way the herdsman stays on the rope, and feel exactly where it tugs, in the hands, the chest, the jaw. Then come back to the breath, and when it pulls again, stay again.
Catching the ox. The fourth oxherding picture: the herdsman gets the ox on a rope, and the ox, long wild, fights it. Today's word.

1225.title: Taming the ox
1225.hook: fifth picture: patiently, the ox is tamed
1225.howItsDone: Zen students often describe their daily sitting with the language of the fifth oxherding picture: noticing the mind wander and returning it, over and over, as the slow work of training.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth picture: the ox on a rope at last, and fighting it. Your line: it pulls.

Every step so far has been about finding or grabbing. A search through the grass, tracks in the mud, a glimpse among green willows, a rope pulled tight as the ox bolted for the hills. The fifth picture is different. Nothing is grabbed. It's about time. And it ties together a week that ran like one road, starting with Huineng: a robe no longer handed down, then meditation and wisdom as one, like a lamp and its light.
screen: `SEARCHING, TRACKS, A GLIMPSE, A ROPE.` → `NOW: TIME.` → `A LAMP AND ITS LIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, one thought, then another. The preface, in paraphrase, says that when one thought arises, another follows right behind it. The ox wandering off isn't one big escape; it's a chain of small ones. And the preface says these come up from the mind, not from the surroundings. The fields aren't the problem. The wandering is. Second, keep the rope close. The verse says he keeps whip and rope near, in case the ox strays back into the dust. Not panic: the plain attention of someone who has done this every day for a while. He no longer chases the ox across the valley. He notices the first step away and turns it back. Third, gentle, it follows untied. Well tended, the verse says, the ox grows gentle and follows him on its own. No single great insight did that, no heroic effort. Just the same small returning, again and again, until returning is the ox's habit too. Fourth, patience is the method. Yesterday was grip; today is the long middle, the part of any practice that doesn't make a good story: the hundredth time back to the breath, the morning you sit anyway. That's the week's thread. Huineng's lamp and light are one; the glimpse and the training aren't two. The ox isn't tamed by force. It's tamed by being met, patiently, every time it wanders.
screen: `ONE THOUGHT, THEN ANOTHER.` · `KEEP THE ROPE CLOSE.` · `GENTLE, IT FOLLOWS UNTIED.` · `PATIENCE IS THE METHOD.` · then, large: `TAMED.`

segments.voice: Rest with the breath, and watch for the moment one thought hooks the next, the ox's first step toward the dust. When you notice, come back gently, without a speech to yourself about wandering, and do it again, counting nothing, scoring nothing. Let the returning be easy, the way a hand keeps a rope loose but near.
Taming the ox. The fifth oxherding picture: through patient, daily attention, the wild ox grows gentle and follows without a rope. Today's word.
Your line: tamed. Gentle now, the ox follows without a rope. That's today, done.
